titleStmt.title: Corticostriatal neurons in auditory cortex drive decisions during auditory discrimination
titleStmt.author: Znamenskiy
Zador

bibl.title: Corticostriatal neurons in auditory cortex drive decisions during auditory discrimination

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether the projection from auditory cortex to striatum carries the signals that drive choices during auditory discrimination
span.quote: We hypothesized that the projection from the auditory cortex to the striatum carries acoustic information that drives behavioural choices during auditory discrimination.

span.label: how auditory representations in cortex are transformed into motor commands
span.quote: The neural pathways by which information about the acoustic world reaches the auditory cortex are well characterised, but how auditory representations are transformed into motor commands is not known.

span.label: shows that activating corticostriatal neurons biases choices toward their preferred frequency and inactivating them biases choices away, establishing the pathway as both sufficient and necessary for the decision
span.quote: Targeted Channelrhodopsin-2 1 , 2 (ChR2)-mediated stimulation of corticostriatal neurones during the task biased decisions in the direction predicted by the frequency tuning of the stimulated neurones, whereas archaerhodopsin-3 3 (Arch)-mediated inactivation biased decisions in the opposite direction.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: We directly demonstrate the role of corticostriatal projection neurones in auditory decisions by specifically manipulating the activity of these neurones in rats performing an auditory frequency discrimination task.

span.label: auditory perceptual decision-making
span.quote: We hypothesized that the projection from the auditory cortex to the striatum carries acoustic information that drives behavioural choices during auditory discrimination.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: We used tetrode recordings to characterize the activity of individual neurones in the auditory cortex and the auditory striatum while rats performed the task.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: We hypothesized that the projection from the auditory cortex to the striatum carries acoustic information that drives behavioural choices during auditory discrimination.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: Excitation of corticostriatal neurones resulted in general suppression of local cortical activity ( Fig. S6 ), favouring the hypothesis that behavioural effects of photostimulation are mediated by long-range rather than local outputs of these neurones.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: Our results suggest that the finite bandwidth provided by a small number of projection neurones that drive decisions constitutes an additional constraint limiting the effective pool size and therefore psychophysical performance.

span.label: sufficiency and necessity are separated explicitly, and the direction of the necessity test is predicted before it is run
span.quote: If corticostriatal spikes are important under normal conditions, then suppressing these spikes during the task should lead to an “anti-bias,” i.e. a bias in the direction opposite that induced by ChR2 activation.

span.label: cell-type specificity is achieved by an intersection: a retrograde virus delivers Cre from the target region, and a Cre-dependent virus supplies the opsin in the source region
span.quote: In the first strategy, we targeted ChR2 specifically to corticostriatal neurones using a Herpes Simplex Virus-1 (HSV1) engineered to express Cre recombinase 19 , 20 , 21 ( Fig. 2a ). This virus, when injected into the auditory striatum, was transported retrogradely along the axons and drove Cre expression in corticostriatal neurones. We then injected a Cre-dependent AAV driving expression of ChR2 into the auditory cortex, resulting in expression of ChR2 only in neurones infected by both the HSV1-Cre and the AAV-ChR2.

span.label: a failed non-specific manipulation is reported first, with three candidate explanations, and becomes the argument for targeting
span.quote: The lack of correspondence between the direction of stimulation-evoked choice biases and frequency tuning was surprising and has several possible explanations. First, these choice biases may result from activation of intracortical projection neurones from other frequency bands of the auditory cortex. Second, they may arise from preferential activation of local interneurones in response to synchronous activation of a large number of cortical cells. Third, these biases may be a consequence of stimulation of competing output pathways, projecting to target areas with different functional roles.

span.label: full inactivation is deliberately avoided because compensatory plasticity would confound it, so only a patch of the tonotopic map is silenced
span.quote: Rather than attempting to inactivate all corticostriatal cells—a technically difficult feat whose interpretation might be obscured by the compensatory plasticity common to lesion studies—we sought instead to silence corticostriatal neurones within a restricted region of the tonotopic map.

span.label: the same pathway is driven at two points - somata in cortex and axon terminals in striatum - so the result cannot depend on where the light went
span.quote: Thus both direct activation of corticostriatal somata in the cortex, as well as antidromic activation of corticostriatal terminals in the striatum, biased the rats’ choices in a manner predicted from the frequency tuning of the activated neurones.

span.label: recurrent cortical activity is pharmacologically removed while the axons are stimulated, which isolates the long-range output as the carrier of the effect
span.quote: Photostimulation of corticostriatal axons still biased choices in the absence of cortical activity ( p = 0.016, signed-rank test, Fig. S8,S9 ), demonstrating that these biases are mediated directly by long-range outputs of corticostriatal neurones.

span.label: the behavioural effect is converted into stimulus units by fitting a logistic model, so a neural manipulation and an acoustic change become comparable
span.quote: To quantify the effects of photostimulation on subjects’ behaviour, we fit a logistic regression model to the subjects’ choices (see Methods), estimating what change to the auditory stimulus would produce a behavioural effect equivalent to that of photostimulation.

span.label: stimulation is restricted to a quarter of trials and still rewarded normally, to stop the animal adapting to the manipulation itself
span.quote: To minimize behavioural adaptation to photostimulation we limited the number of stimulation trials to 25%, and rewarded the animal as on control trials according to the frequency content of the stimulus.

span.label: tone intensity is randomised across trials specifically to block a loudness-based strategy
span.quote: To discourage subjects from using loudness differences in discrimination, tone intensity was randomly selected on each trial from a uniform distribution 45–75 dB (SPL) during training.

span.label: the effect size is tied to an anatomical count by combining fluorescence, a measured inactivation space constant, and cell density
span.quote: Robust choice biases were observed for sites with 1040–2444 Arch-expressing neurones within 1 mm of the fiber, comprising 0.35–0.83% of neurones in that volume.

span.label: uninjected animals receiving identical light serve as the control for both opsins separately
span.quote: Choice biases were not observed in uninjected controls ( Fig. 2g , S5a ) indicating that they were driven by the ChR2-mediated activation of corticostriatal neurones and not non-specific effects of light delivery.

span.label: local suppression during corticostriatal excitation is used to argue the behavioural effect travels by the long-range output rather than through local circuitry
span.quote: Excitation of corticostriatal neurones resulted in general suppression of local cortical activity ( Fig. S6 ), favouring the hypothesis that behavioural effects of photostimulation are mediated by long-range rather than local outputs of these neurones.

span.label: Non-specific cortical activation did not give tuning-predicted biases and lacked adequate control over the relevant projection neurons.
span.quote: These results suggested that the auditory cortex plays a role in the task, but that the method of non-specific activation of diverse neuronal populations used in these experiments does not provide sufficient experimental control over the activity of the projection neurones driving choices in this behaviour.

span.label: The stimulation biases were not statistically significant within individual sessions.
span.quote: The biases were not significant on individual sessions (p<0.05 on 1/33 sessions), in part because the number of stimulated trials per session was typically small (70±24 (s.d.) trials).

span.label: The inactivation effect on chronometric functions did not reach significance.
span.quote: A similar trend was reflected in the subjects’ chronometric functions but did not reach significance ( Fig. S11kl ).

span.label: Cell counts could not be estimated for two fibres whose tracks were not found histologically.
span.quote: For 2 fibers in one of the rats we could not locate the tracks in histological sections and precisely estimate cell counts.

span.label: Other parallel pathways contributing to the decision are not excluded.
span.quote: While our results do not exclude the participation of other parallel pathways, the ubiquity of corticostriatal projections in cortex may provide a general mechanism for control of motor decisions by sensory context 27 .

span.quote: Stimulation also had a modest effect on the subjects’ performance at sites with large choice biases, possibly due to a ceiling effect

span.quote: By contrast, the function of striatal regions which receive direct input from sensory cortical areas is less well established.

span.quote: We trained rats to discriminate low and high frequency “cloud-of-tones” stimuli in a two alternative choice task

span.quote: These observations indicate that neurones in the striatum preserve the information available to perform the ”cloud-of-tones” task.

span.label: a retrogradely transported herpes virus carrying Cre, which turns an anatomical projection into a genetically addressable cell class
span.quote: In the first strategy, we targeted ChR2 specifically to corticostriatal neurones using a Herpes Simplex Virus-1 (HSV1) engineered to express Cre recombinase 19 , 20 , 21 ( Fig. 2a ). This virus, when injected into the auditory striatum, was transported retrogradely along the axons and drove Cre expression in corticostriatal neurones. We then injected a Cre-dependent AAV driving expression of ChR2 into the auditory cortex, resulting in expression of ChR2 only in neurones infected by both the HSV1-Cre and the AAV-ChR2.

span.label: sufficiency versus necessity - activation showing the pathway CAN drive choices, inactivation showing it normally DOES; the paper separates the two claims and tests them in that order
span.quote: Our results so far establish that activation of the corticostriatal pathway is sufficient to bias subjects’ choices during an auditory discrimination task, but do not establish whether corticostriatal activity contributes to the formation of decisions under normal conditions, in the absence of ChR2 activation.

span.label: stimulating the pathway at the soma versus at the axon terminal; the same cells reached from either end, which is what rules out a location artefact
span.quote: Thus both direct activation of corticostriatal somata in the cortex, as well as antidromic activation of corticostriatal terminals in the striatum, biased the rats’ choices in a manner predicted from the frequency tuning of the activated neurones.

span.label: a behavioural effect measured as a choice bias versus as a shift in response time; the chronometric curve moves as if acoustic evidence had been added

The redundancy arising from correlated neuronal firing may restrict the effective size of the pool 26 , limiting psychophysical performance.
